sources.headline: Pope does not need further treatment after lung cancer surgery
sources.text: Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said.Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican."A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added.The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds.It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday.The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung.The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.He said at the time that it had been caught "at an early stage".Images shared days after his operation, on Friday, showed the Pope celebrating Mass from the hospital wearing green vestments and standing behind a makeshift altar.On the same day, the Vatican said he spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone to urge a ceasefire in the blockaded Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow the delivery of food aid, and to call for "dialogue and peace".The pontiff had a similar phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.Those close to the Pope have also previously said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America which is planned for early November.

sources.headline: Pope Leo needs no further treatment after cancer surgery, doctors say
sources.text: The 71-year-old leader of the Catholic church has had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery.Pope Leo XIV needs no further treatment for lung cancer after confirming the disease had not spread following recent surgery, the Vatican announced in a statement from doctors.“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said Wednesday.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican sayslist 2 of 3Pope Leo resumes work in hospital while recovering from surgerylist 3 of 3Pope Leo to make public appearance Sunday, first since cancer surgeryend of listThe 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung surgically removed on October 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Leo was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli Polyclinic on Saturday, four days after his operation, and the Vatican said he would gradually resume his activities. On Wednesday, he returned to St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with pilgrims.Pope Leo XIV greets cardinals as he arrives for the weekly general audience at St Peter’s Square in the Vatican on October 21, 2026 [Tiziana Fabi/AFP]Found by chanceAdditional treatment is generally offered in cases where follow-up testing finds signs that the cancer has spread, such as through the lymph nodes, or if other signs indicate that it might be particularly aggressive. Surgery often can be enough when tumours are caught very early, as the Catholic leader appears to have had, when the nodule was initially found during another unrelated exam.In an interview with Vatican News on Saturday, Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations, and that the pope had not been experiencing any symptoms.Pope Leo XIV greets the faithful during his weekly general audience in Vatican City on October 21, 2026 [Fabio Frustaci/EPA]The pope carried on his official business while in the hospital, including a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. He has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St Peter’s Square and Wednesday’s longer audience in the square, greeting the faithful from around the world.“Thank you! Thank you for the support of your prayers,” Leo exclaimed to the audience.It appears that the Catholic leader remains committed to his November 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.Leo’s lead surgeon told Vatican News that there was “no clinical reason” to prevent the trip, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and high-altitude stops.

Pope Leo XIV will need no further treatment after his surgery for lung cancer, his doctors announced on Wednesday.

The pope’s personal doctor and the surgeon who removed a lower lobe of the pope’s right lung at Gemelli Hospital in Rome on Oct. 13 said in a statement that follow-up tests confirmed that the cancer was localized.

“A subsequent oncology evaluation confirmed that no further treatment is necessary,” the doctors wrote.

The announcement came eight days after the pontiff’s diagnosis was revealed publicly, casting his agenda into uncertainty some 18 months into his papacy.

sources.text:
Pope Leo XIV

Copyright AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia
By Euronews
Published on
21/10/2026 - 22:49 GMT+2
Share
The pontiff needs no further treatment, his doctors said, eight days after an hour-and-a-half operation on his right lung.
Final histological tests and molecular biology analyses carried out on tissue removed during Pope Leo XIV’s surgery have confirmed the presence of a localised pulmonary adenocarcinoma.
A subsequent oncological assessment has determined that no further therapy is necessary.
The update was given by the Pope’s doctors, Dr Luigi Carbone and Prof Stefano Margaritora, as they reported on the pontiff’s postoperative progress.
The examinations confirmed that the disease had not spread beyond the lung. In light of these results and the specialist evaluation, no additional oncological treatment has been deemed necessary.
It was the Pope himself who, during the Angelus prayer on 11 October, revealed that he had a nodule in his right lung. He was then admitted to hospital and underwent surgery on 13 October, in an operation lasting around an hour and a half.

Associated Press
Published: 4:23am, 22 Oct 2026Updated: 4:58am, 22 Oct 2026

Pope Leo needs no further treatment for lung cancer after follow-up tests confirmed the disease was localised, the Vatican said in a statement on Wednesday.

Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

He left the hospital on Saturday, four days after surgery and well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated.

The pope’s personal doctor, Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the final post-operative tests on tissue removed during the pope’s surgery confirmed the initial diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread.

“A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary,” the doctors said.

01:58
Filipino Catholics pray for Pope Leo’s recovery after lung cancer surgery

The pope had the lower section, or lobe, of his right lung removed to try to ensure that all the cancer was removed.

Additional treatment is offered in such cases if follow-up testing finds signs that the cancer has spread or has certain other signs that it might be particularly aggressive.

Surgery often can be enough when tumours are caught very early, such as when someone has an X-ray or other scan that shows a spot long before it is large or causing symptoms.

The pope appears to have had one of those “incidental findings”, a nodule in his lung spotted during another exam.

In an interview with Vatican News, Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations.

The pope carried on business while in hospital, including a call with Russian President Putin, and has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St Peter’s Square and Wednesday’s longer audience, when he greeted the faithful from all over the world.

His next major engagement is an ambitious November 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

Margaritora was quoted by Vatican News as saying that there was “no clinical reason” to prevent the trip, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and high altitude stops.

The pope revealed that a nodule had been found and would be surgically removed during the traditional Sunday blessing on October 11, in an unusually transparent disclosure.

sources.headline: Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment, doctors say
sources.text: VATICAN CITY - Pope Leo will not need any further therapy after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week, his doctors said on Oct 21, indicating that his tumour had not spread.The announcement came as it was still unclear whether the US-born pope would proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for Nov 6-17.The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on Oct 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.Final histological examinations and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed confirmed the diagnosis, with the disease remaining localised, the doctors said in a statement released by the Vatican.“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said.Leo was discharged from hospital on Oct 17 and is gradually resuming his normal duties.On Oct 21, he returned to St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with pilgrims.Margaritora said last week there were “no clinical reasons” preventing the pope from travelling to South America, but the Vatican’s secretary of state has indicated the pontiff may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid his recovery. sources.headline: Pope Leo says he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
sources.text:
Pope Leo XIV appears at the window of his study in the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter's Square at the Vatican for the traditional noon blessing after praying the Angelus, Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, a day after he returned from the hospital, where he had lung cancer removed on Tuesday.
Alessandra Tarantino/AP
hide caption
Alessandra Tarantino/AP
VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties. The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed. ''Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.
The pontiff said the experience of the last week "has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity." He told the faithful that he had ''truly felt your support,'' and expressed ''particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli hospital'' where he was treated. The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace. A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing. ''He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″ The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He told a reporter in English that he was doing ''much better'' as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated. "I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. "It is a miracle that he recovered already."
American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization. ''I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,'' Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.'' Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock. "I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said. Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place." "The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so." Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.

sources.headline: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer as growth removed during surgery
sources.text: Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican said late on Tuesday.Leo, 71, underwent an operation and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, with tests confirming a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, which followed an earlier statement saying the pope’s operation had concluded “successfully, on schedule and as planned”.The Vatican added that the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.Leo was in the operating theatre for about three hours and the operation itself lasted approximately 90 minutes.In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, Leo said during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup, adding that it was “well-contained” and detected early.“The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it,” he said to the crowds gathered in St Peter’s Square.Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, is being treated in Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where a large crowd greeted his arrival earlier on Tuesday.The Vatican said that Leo had “now returned to his room” following the operation.All of his appointments have been cancelled until 20 October.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, a practicing Catholic who has met with the pope, said he and his wife were “united in prayers” for Leo following the diagnosis. The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, also wished him a quick recovery, saying he was “a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world.”Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said he had seen Leo on Monday night. “We spoke with great serenity,” Parolin told Rai News. “He is truly a great example. The announcement came like a bolt out of the blue, nobody expected it. Thank God it was detected immediately, so the operation could take place immediately. Normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved.”Leo is staying in the 10th-floor private-patient wing but not in the papal suite, which is being renovated.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionThe Chicago-born pope, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, is generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.Leo travelled to France on a papal visit in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.The weekly papal audience on Wednesday will be led by Luis Antonio Tagle, a cardinal from the Philippines who last week was elected dean of the college of cardinals – the authority that presides over papal conclaves.The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish the high-security papal suite.Leo’s predecessor, Francis, spent more than five weeks in the hospital, being treated for bronchitis, which developed into bilateral pneumonia. He died at home in Casa Santa Marta in Vatican City on 21 April 2025, just under a month after being discharged.

Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer after doctors successfully remove nodule 
 
  Europe   
 Pope ​Leo had a lower lobe ​of his right lung removed during surgery on Tuesday ​and ‌was diagnosed with lung ⁠adenocarcinoma, a common form of ‌lung cancer, the Vatican said in ⁠a medical bulletin. The surgery was successful and the pope is expected to spend a week in hospital recovering. The 71-year-old pontiff is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on November 6, though the Vatican has not confirmed the operation date.

"The procedure was successfully completed, within the expected time and in the planned manner, and the Holy Father has returned to his room," the Vatican press office said on Telegram. 
The 71-year-old pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the ​bulletin said. 
Pope Leo arrived at hospital in Rome on Tuesday ahead of surgery to remove ​a small cancerous growth on one of his lungs, in the first major health issue of his 17-month tenure.  
Leo, 71, said on Sunday that a small nodule had been ​found on a ‌check-up, was "well-contained" and had been spotted early. 
He was ⁠expected to leave the Vatican for Rome's Gemelli hospital late morning, the Vatican press office said, without specifying when ‌the actual operation would take place. 
Leo, elected by the world's cardinals ⁠in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker ​or to have had health issues previously. 
The Vatican has said ‌his recovery is expected to take about a week. All his public events have been cancelled until October 20.

A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion ‌that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although ​risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking. 
Dr. Federico Venuto, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome's Policlinico Umberto I hospital, said procedures to ​remove lung nodules are usually minimally invasive, and can sometimes involve use of a ​thin camera tube called a thoracoscope. 
"The complication rate ​is extremely low," he told Reuters. 
Read morePope Leo says will undergo surgery for early-stage lung nodule 
The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, died at age 88 in April 2025 and ​was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. 
Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of ⁠Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17. 
In the same address on Sunday when the ⁠pope announced his need ​for surgery, Leo pledged he would go forward with the trip. 
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)
